question: Identify the form of payment Priya is using.

points: Standing order (1)

question: State two differences between a standing order and a direct debit.

points: Standing order: fixed amount; direct debit: variable amount (1)
Standing order: set by the consumer; direct debit: set by the recipient organisation (1)
Standing order: consumer can change it at any time; direct debit: organisation controls the amount taken (1)

Allows them to plan and save for future goals (1)

Level of income / wealth (1)

Personal confidence / experience with investing (1)

Auto-enrolment means eligible workers are signed up automatically (1)
Tax relief on contributions (1)
Funds are invested and grow over time (1)

scenario: Chloe has £3,000 she wants to put away for five years and does not need access to it. She is trying to decide between a regular savings account and a fixed-rate bond.
question: Explain one advantage to Chloe of choosing a fixed-rate bond rather than a regular savings account.

mark_scheme.instruction: Award 1 mark for the point and 1 mark for development/application.
points: A fixed-rate bond typically offers a higher rate of interest than a regular savings account (1) which means Chloe will earn more interest on her £3,000 over the five-year period (1)
The interest rate is fixed for the term (1) so Chloe knows exactly how much she will earn and is protected if rates fall (1)
mark_scheme.additional_guidance: Must apply to Chloe's situation for second mark.

scenario: Chloe has £3,000 she wants to put away for five years and does not need access to it. She is trying to decide between a regular savings account and a fixed-rate bond.
question: Explain one disadvantage to Chloe of choosing a fixed-rate bond.

mark_scheme.instruction: Award 1 mark for point and 1 mark for development/application.
points: A fixed-rate bond locks money away for a set period (1) so if Chloe needs emergency access to her £3,000 she will face a penalty or be unable to withdraw (1)
If interest rates rise during the five years (1) Chloe cannot benefit from higher rates as her rate is fixed (1)

scenario: Marcus is 24 and needs to borrow £1,500 to buy a laptop for his freelance work. He is considering a personal loan at 8.9% APR repaid over 2 years, or a credit card at 22.9% APR.
question: Explain two advantages to Marcus of using a personal loan rather than a credit card for this purchase.

mark_scheme.instruction: Award 1 mark for each point and 1 mark for each development. Maximum 4 marks (2 advantages).
points: The personal loan has a lower APR (8.9% vs 22.9%) (1) meaning Marcus will pay less in interest over the two years, reducing the total cost of borrowing (1)
A personal loan has a fixed repayment schedule (1) so Marcus knows exactly how much he will pay each month, making budgeting easier (1)
A personal loan has a definite end date (1) whereas a credit card minimum repayment can extend the debt for many years (1)
mark_scheme.additional_guidance: Award a maximum of 2 advantages. Both point and development needed for each 2-mark award.

topic: A3 Life stages and financial needs
scenario: Fatima is 45, has two children in secondary school, and is thinking about her financial priorities for the next ten years.
question: Explain two financial priorities Fatima should consider at her life stage.

mark_scheme.instruction: Award 1 mark for each priority and 1 mark for development. Maximum 4 marks.
points: Increasing pension contributions (1) as she has roughly 20 years until retirement and the more she contributes now the larger her retirement fund will be (1)
Building an emergency fund / rainy day savings (1) because with children and a mortgage she needs a buffer against unexpected costs such as redundancy or car repairs (1)
Paying down any mortgage (1) to reduce debt before retirement so she has lower outgoings in old age (1)
Starting to save for children's education / university costs (1) to avoid her children needing large student loans (1)
mark_scheme.additional_guidance: Award a maximum of 2 priorities. Accept any financially relevant priority linked to her life stage.

scenario: Hamid runs a small market stall selling homemade jams and would like to accept card payments as well as cash.
question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage to Hamid of accepting card payments.

mark_scheme.instruction: Award 1+1 for advantage and 1+1 for disadvantage.
points: Advantage: Customers who do not carry cash can still make a purchase (1) which could increase Hamid's sales and revenue (1)
Disadvantage: There is usually a transaction fee charged by the card processor (1) which reduces Hamid's profit margin on each sale (1)
Disadvantage: Requires card reader hardware and internet connectivity (1) which adds upfront cost for Hamid and could fail at the stall (1)
mark_scheme.additional_guidance: Must have one clear advantage and one clear disadvantage for full marks.

scenario: Yemi and her partner are first-time buyers looking at mortgages. They are deciding between a fixed-rate mortgage and a variable-rate tracker mortgage.
question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage to Yemi of choosing a fixed-rate mortgage.

mark_scheme.instruction: Award 1+1 for advantage and 1+1 for disadvantage.
points: Advantage: Monthly payments stay the same throughout the fixed period (1) making budgeting easier and protecting Yemi if the Bank of England raises interest rates (1)
Disadvantage: If interest rates fall, Yemi is locked into a higher fixed rate (1) so she would pay more than she would on a tracker mortgage (1)
Disadvantage: Early repayment charges often apply if she wants to switch (1) making the mortgage less flexible (1)

scenario: Daniel earns £1,800 per month after tax. His regular outgoings are rent £650, food £250, transport £120, and phone £40.
question: Explain one action Daniel could take to improve his financial position based on this information.

mark_scheme.instruction: Award 1 mark for action and 1 mark for development.
points: Daniel has £740 left after essential outgoings (1) and could set up a standing order to move a fixed amount into savings each month to build an emergency fund (1)
Daniel could review his transport costs (1) and consider whether a cheaper option such as cycling or a bus pass could reduce this and free up more disposable income (1)
mark_scheme.additional_guidance: Accept any sensible, contextually applied action.

question: Explain why payday loans are considered a high-risk borrowing option for consumers.

mark_scheme.instruction: Award 1 mark for reason and 1 mark for development.
points: Payday loans carry very high APR rates often exceeding 1,000% (1) meaning if the borrower cannot repay on the due date the debt can grow very quickly (1)
They are designed as short-term solutions (1) but if the consumer cannot repay they may need to take another loan, leading to a debt spiral (1)

question: Explain why a person's attitude to financial risk is likely to change as they get older.

mark_scheme.instruction: Award 1 mark for reason and 1 mark for development.
points: Older people typically have fewer working years ahead (1) so they have less time to recover from investment losses and cannot afford to take high risks with savings needed for retirement (1)
As people approach retirement they often switch to lower-risk investments (1) to protect the capital they have accumulated rather than seeking high growth (1)

scenario: Beatrice is 30 and has just bought her first home with a £180,000 mortgage. She is considering whether to take out life insurance.
question: Explain two reasons why Beatrice should consider taking out life insurance at this stage.

mark_scheme.instruction: Award 1+1 for each reason. Maximum 4 marks.
points: Life insurance would pay out if Beatrice died during the policy term (1) covering the remaining mortgage debt so her family does not lose the house (1)
As a first-time buyer she has taken on significant debt (1) and life insurance provides financial security for any dependants who rely on her income (1)
Premiums are lower when taken out at a younger age (1) so starting at 30 means Beatrice can secure cheaper cover than if she waits (1)

question: Explain two advantages to a consumer of using a cash ISA compared with a standard savings account.

mark_scheme.instruction: Award 1+1 for each advantage. Maximum 4 marks.
points: Interest earned in a cash ISA is tax-free (1) whereas interest in a standard savings account may be subject to income tax if it exceeds the Personal Savings Allowance (1)
ISA savings can be carried forward each year (1) building a growing tax-free pot without losing the tax benefit on past savings (1)

scenario: A law firm needs to transfer £85,000 to a client the same day to complete a property purchase.
question: Explain why the law firm would use CHAPS rather than BACS for this payment.

mark_scheme.instruction: Award 1+1 for each reason. Maximum 4 marks.
points: CHAPS is a same-day payment system (1) so the funds will arrive in the client's account on the same day, which is essential for completing the property purchase (1)
BACS typically takes 2–3 working days (1) which would delay the transaction and could cause the property deal to fall through (1)
CHAPS handles large-value transfers securely (1) making it suitable for the £85,000 involved (1)
mark_scheme.additional_guidance: Award a maximum of 2 points. Must reference speed or same-day processing.

topic: A3 Life stages and financial needs
scenario: Jemma is 17 and has just started her first part-time job earning £200 per month.
question: Explain two steps Jemma could take to start managing her personal finances effectively.

mark_scheme.instruction: Award 1+1 for each step. Maximum 4 marks.
points: Open a current account (1) so she can receive her wages by BACS and use a debit card for everyday spending rather than carrying cash (1)
Create a simple monthly budget (1) listing her income and planned spending so she can see how much she has available to save (1)
Set up a regular savings account or ISA (1) and save a fixed amount each month by standing order to build up a fund for future goals (1)

scenario: Kwame, aged 25, has just started his first full-time job. He has been automatically enrolled in the company pension scheme but is considering opting out to have more take-home pay.
question: Explain two reasons why Kwame should remain in the company pension scheme.

mark_scheme.instruction: Award 1+1 for each reason. Maximum 4 marks.
points: The employer contributes to the pension (1) so if Kwame opts out he loses effectively 'free' money that boosts his retirement savings (1)
Starting at 25 gives the fund a long time to grow through investment (1) and compound growth means even small contributions can become significant by retirement age (1)
Contributions attract tax relief (1) so the government effectively tops up every £100 Kwame contributes (1)

scenario: Sofia is a university student who has a £1,200 credit card balance at 21.9% APR. She has been offered a 0% balance transfer card for 18 months with a 3% transfer fee.
question: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage to Sofia of transferring her balance to the new card.

mark_scheme.instruction: Award 1+1 for advantage and 1+1 for disadvantage.
points: Advantage: The 0% period means Sofia pays no interest for 18 months (1) allowing the full monthly payment to reduce the outstanding balance rather than paying interest (1)
Disadvantage: There is a 3% transfer fee on the balance (1) which amounts to £36 on £1,200 and must be paid upfront (1)
Disadvantage: If Sofia does not clear the balance within 18 months (1) she will be charged interest at whatever the card's standard rate is, which could be higher than her current 21.9% (1)

scenario: Morgan is 23 with a £2,000 credit card balance at 19.9% APR and a £1,000 car loan at 7% APR with 12 months remaining. He has been offered a new 0% balance transfer card for 12 months, rising to 29.9% after. There is no transfer fee.
question: Discuss whether Morgan should transfer his debts to the new credit card. (6)

mark_scheme.instruction: Levels-based. Award marks holistically for the quality of discussion, balance, use of evidence and conclusion.
indicative_content: Saves interest on the £2,000 credit card balance at 19.9% during the 12-month 0% period
Car loan at 7% ends in 12 months anyway — minimal interest saving from transferring it
29.9% after 12 months is higher than both current rates — significant risk if not cleared
No transfer fee makes it more worthwhile
Good option if Morgan is disciplined enough to clear the balance within 12 months
Not suitable if Morgan is likely to overspend on the new card and increase his balance
He should prioritise paying off the credit card balance as it is the more expensive debt

level_descriptors.descriptor: Limited discussion; may simply describe the 0% offer or list features without weighing up; little or no context.
Some weighing up — identifies at least one benefit and one risk; partial application to Morgan's circumstances.

Well-developed, balanced discussion; considers cost saving on the credit card, minimal benefit for car loan, risk of 29.9% post-introductory rate; justified conclusion linked to Morgan's specific situation.

topic: A3 Life stages and financial needs
scenario: Josephine is 55 and plans to retire at 65. She has a workplace pension, owns her home outright, and has £20,000 in a cash ISA. Her grown-up children are financially independent.
question: Discuss the extent to which Josephine is financially prepared for retirement. (6)

indicative_content: Strengths: home owned outright — no mortgage in retirement; ISA provides a tax-free emergency fund; workplace pension accumulating
She has 10 years left to contribute more to her pension
Cash ISA may not be growing quickly if interest rates are low compared with inflation
Should consider whether the pension pot will provide sufficient income at retirement
Could consider equity release or downsizing in future if additional income needed
No dependants means lower financial obligations
Conclusion should be supported — fairly well prepared but should review pension projections

level_descriptors.descriptor: Basic description of her assets with little analysis.
Identifies strengths and weaknesses; some development of points.
Balanced discussion using evidence from scenario; well-supported conclusion about her preparedness.

scenario: Takudzwa and his family are travelling to Europe for three weeks. Each family member has a kayak (£400 each, 4 people) and a smartphone (£300 each). He is choosing between two travel insurance policies: Policy X costs £120, covers £1,500 per item up to £3,000 total, includes medical cover and cancellation. Policy Y costs £75, covers £500 per item up to £2,000 total, includes medical but no cancellation cover.
question: Discuss which travel insurance policy Takudzwa should choose. (6)

indicative_content: Total value of kayaks = 4 x £400 = £1,600; smartphones = 4 x £300 = £1,200
Policy X: per-item limit £1,500 covers kayaks and phones; total limit £3,000 sufficient
Policy Y: per-item limit £500 does not cover kayaks (£400 each — actually does) and covers phones (£300 under £500)
Wait — kayaks at £400 each are under Policy Y's £500 per-item limit, so they are covered
Policy Y total limit £2,000: total items = £1,600 + £1,200 = £2,800 — exceeds Policy Y's total limit
Policy X total limit £3,000 covers the full £2,800 value of items
Policy Y has no cancellation cover — relevant if there is any risk of the trip being cancelled
Policy X costs £45 more but provides cancellation cover and higher total limit
Conclusion should weigh cost vs adequate total cover; Policy X appears better value given the high item values

level_descriptors.descriptor: Basic comparison of price or features; no application to item values.
Compares at least two features and begins to apply to Takudzwa's items; partial conclusion.
Thorough analysis using item values and policy limits; considers cancellation; well-supported justified conclusion.

scenario: Rafi is 28 and wants to buy a car worth £8,000. He has three options: a personal loan at 6.9% APR over 3 years, hire purchase through the dealer at 9.9% APR over 3 years, or using his £8,000 savings.
question: Discuss which option Rafi should choose to finance the car. (6)

indicative_content: Using savings: no interest cost — cheapest option; but wipes out emergency fund
Personal loan at 6.9%: retains savings as emergency fund; fixed monthly payments; interest cost over 3 years
HP at 9.9%: higher APR than personal loan so more expensive overall; car not owned until final payment
If Rafi has no other emergency fund, using all savings could be risky
HP may be easier to obtain if credit score is lower
Personal loan: owns the car immediately, cheaper than HP
Balanced conclusion needed: if savings are his only buffer, personal loan may be preferable to preserve emergency fund

level_descriptors.descriptor: Basic description of options; no comparison or application.
Compares at least two options with some development; partial conclusion.
Balanced comparison of all three; considers interest costs, ownership, liquidity; justified, contextualised conclusion.

topic: A5 Attitudes to risk / savings products
scenario: Nia is 40 and has £15,000 to invest. She is considering three options: a cash ISA paying 3.5% AER, a stocks-and-shares ISA with potential returns of 6-8% but risk of capital loss, or a premium bonds account offering a prize-based return equivalent to approximately 4% tax-free.
question: Discuss which savings or investment option best suits Nia's needs. (6)

indicative_content: Cash ISA: guaranteed 3.5% return, tax-free, low risk — suitable for risk-averse saver
Stocks and shares ISA: higher potential return but risk of losing capital — not suitable if she needs certainty
Premium Bonds: tax-free, government-backed, no capital risk but return is variable and prize-based — not everyone wins
At 40 she has time to take some risk if she doesn't need the money soon
If the £15,000 is a significant portion of her savings, capital protection may be a priority
Diversification — could split between products
Inflation erodes real value of cash ISA at 3.5% if inflation is higher
Conclusion should be contextually justified and acknowledge uncertainty

level_descriptors.descriptor: Describes one or two products with minimal comparison.
Compares products and begins to apply to Nia's situation; some reference to risk vs return.
Thorough, balanced comparison; considers risk, return, tax, and Nia's age and circumstances; well-justified conclusion.

scenario: Amara is 35, earns £42,000 per year, and has just received a £20,000 inheritance. She has an outstanding credit card balance of £4,500 at 20.9% APR and no savings. Her employer offers auto-enrolment pension (she is currently opted out). She rents her flat and would like to buy in the next 3 years. [Table: Cash ISA 3.8% AER; Lifetime ISA 25% government bonus, max £4,000/year, accessible at 60 or for first home; Premium Bonds ~4.4% tax-free; Stocks and Shares ISA variable; pay off credit card — saves 20.9% interest]
question: Evaluate how Amara should use her £20,000 inheritance to best improve her financial position. (12)

mark_scheme.instruction: Levels-based, 4 levels. Reward thorough, balanced evaluation with a supported conclusion.
indicative_content: Repaying the credit card (£4,500 at 20.9%): guaranteed 20.9% 'return' by eliminating interest — strongest argument for first use
Lifetime ISA: 25% government bonus on up to £4,000/year towards first home; must be used for property or retirement; penalty for withdrawal otherwise
Cash ISA: 3.8% guaranteed, tax-free, accessible — suitable for emergency fund
Premium Bonds: ~4.4% tax-free, government-backed, no risk but variable
Stocks and Shares ISA: potentially higher long-term return but risk to capital
Joining the pension: employer contributions, tax relief — long-term benefit

Strategy: pay off credit card first (£4,500), invest £4,000 in LISA (max annual allowance) to get £5,000 with bonus, put remaining ~£11,500 in cash ISA or premium bonds as emergency fund and deposit savings
Balanced evaluation should acknowledge trade-offs (risk vs return, accessibility, tax efficiency)
Conclusion must be supported with reasoning from the data

level_descriptors.descriptor: Isolated/generic points about one or two options; little or no application to Amara; basic/no conclusion.
Accurate knowledge of financial products; some linkages and application to Amara's situation; partial evaluation; some conclusion.
Accurate, linked knowledge applied to Amara; balanced evaluation of at least 3 options; considers risk, return and timeline; supported conclusion.

Thorough, well-developed evaluation; considers all major options systematically; specialist vocabulary throughout; prioritises debt repayment and high-bonus products; well-structured, justified conclusion with acknowledgement of uncertainty.

scenario: Omar is 28 and has recently started a well-paid graduate job at £38,000. He has no debts, £5,000 in savings, and no pension. His employer contributes 5% to a pension if he contributes at least 3%. His friend advises him to invest in a stocks-and-shares ISA instead of a pension, arguing that ISAs are more flexible. [Table: Pension — employer 5%, tax relief on contributions, locked until ~57; ISA — no employer match, no lock-in, tax-free growth, flexible withdrawal; property investment — higher returns possible but illiquid and requires mortgage]
question: Evaluate whether Omar should prioritise a pension, an ISA or a property investment to build his long-term wealth. (12)

indicative_content: Pension: employer match means 8% of salary invested for 3% cost — substantial benefit; tax relief boosts contributions further; locked until 57 reduces flexibility
ISA: flexible access, no employer match, tax-free growth; good for medium-term goals
Property: high potential returns; requires mortgage and deposit; illiquid; landlord responsibilities
At 28, long investment horizon means compound growth strongly favours pension
Not using the employer contribution is equivalent to a 5% salary reduction
ISA is not an either/or — can have both pension and ISA
Property is high risk and requires more capital
Balanced conclusion: prioritise pension to capture employer match; supplement with ISA; property longer-term

level_descriptors.descriptor: Basic description of one or two options; limited application; generic/no conclusion.
Some accurate knowledge; comparison of at least two options; partial application to Omar; some conclusion.
Balanced evaluation of all three options; applies employer match, tax relief and timescales to Omar; supported conclusion.
Thorough, well-argued evaluation; specialist vocabulary; fully developed reasoning about compound growth, opportunity cost of not joining pension, flexibility needs; clear, well-justified conclusion.

scenario: Laila is 55 and has recently been made redundant. She has a defined contribution pension pot of £150,000, £30,000 in a cash ISA, and no mortgage. She is weighing up: taking early retirement; returning to part-time work; or withdrawing a lump sum from her pension to start a small business. [Table: Pension — can access at 55 under current rules, 25% tax-free lump sum, rest taxed as income; ISA — accessible, tax-free; Business start-up — potential income but risky and costs money]
question: Evaluate the best course of action for Laila given her financial circumstances. (12)

indicative_content: Taking early retirement: has assets but £150k pension and £30k ISA may not provide sufficient income for 30+ retirement years
Sustainability of early retirement — State Pension not until 67; need to calculate annual income needed
Part-time work: provides income while pension keeps growing; less pressure on savings; sensible middle ground
Pension withdrawal for business: takes capital that has been growing tax-sheltered; business risky; could lose retirement savings
25% tax-free lump sum if she takes pension cash — but taxed portion counts as income and could push her into higher rate
ISA as emergency/income buffer; should not be exhausted for business venture
Conclusion: part-time work appears most financially prudent; preserves pension for longer and reduces risk

level_descriptors.descriptor: Basic description of options with limited analysis; generic conclusion.
Identifies financial implications of at least two options; some application to Laila's circumstances.
Balanced evaluation of all three options; considers sustainability, tax implications and risk; supported conclusion.
Thorough, well-developed analysis; considers State Pension gap, tax on lump sum, business risk, longevity risk; specialist vocabulary; clear, justified conclusion with acknowledgement of trade-offs.
